screens.title: Meet Jack — a simple Java-like teaching language
screens.narratorSegment: Jack is the small, Java-like language used throughout this course to teach compilation and object-oriented design. It gives you familiar ideas — classes, methods, constructors, arrays — but keeps the syntax and feature set deliberately minimal so you can build a compiler for it by hand. In practical terms, Jack programs are split into. jack files, each defining a class with fields and methods. That simplicity makes Jack an ideal learning target: you can write a game such as Pong using Jack, compile it to VM code, then to machine code, and see how high-level ideas become concrete instructions. A concrete example is the Main class that calls Output. printInt to display values. A common misconception is that a small language cannot express complex algorithms — in fact Jack is Turing-complete, so brevity does not mean weakness; Jack just limits surface complexity so implementation stays feasible. As you move through these screens you will learn Jack's types, variable kinds, method categories, object construction, and how the Jack OS supplies basic services. Think about this question as we start: what is the smallest set of language features you need to express a complete program?

keyIdea.title: Why Jack matters
keyIdea.text: Jack is small by design so students can implement a full compiler and learn how high-level constructs map to VM operations.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › The Jack Programming Language
The Jack Programming Language
A compact, Java-like language used as the high-level input to the course toolchain.
Jack keeps syntax and features minimal so you can implement a working compiler and explore how classes, objects, and methods become VM commands. We will use Jack programs, the Jack OS, and the VM to understand compilation end-to-end.
Classes
Objects
OS Services
Explore Key Topics
Types, objects, and the small OS that make Jack both teachable and capable.
Classes as blueprints
Think of each class as a building blueprint. Fields are the rooms, methods are the actions you can perform, and a constructor builds the house and returns its address.
Objects as houses
Each object is a contiguous memory block whose base address is passed as this. The OS provides utilities like Output and Memory for working with programs.
Key Takeaway

Jack is intentionally small so you can trace every language feature through a student-built compiler to the VM and hardware.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Describe & Understand
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives describe the core knowledge you will build. First, you will be able to describe Jack's syntax and semantics: that means naming its primitive types, the role of classes and methods, and how source files map to classes. As an example, you should be able to read a simple class file and identify fields, methods, and constructors. Second, you will understand Jack's type system: int, boolean, char, arrays, and objects, and why Jack restricts itself to a small set. Being able to explain the type choices helps you see how compilers perform type checking and memory layout. A common misconception is to assume small type systems are too weak; instead, they simplify compilation while remaining expressive. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify your understanding by reading a short Jack file and tracing variable storage. Practice by opening a Main. jack file, locating each declaration, and describing the storage class. That active check helps cement the objective before you move to applying Jack in programs.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Apply & Build
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on what you will be able to do. First, you will write simple Jack programs using variables, expressions, and control structures and compile them to VM code. A practical check is to write a calculator program and compare the generated VM commands for each Jack statement. Second, you will explain and use Jack's object features: write classes with fields and constructors, create objects, and call methods that use this. The constructor pattern—allocating memory and returning this—is important, and you will see how it appears in the VM code. A typical misconception is to equate Jack classes with full Java classes including inheritance; Jack deliberately omits inheritance and polymorphism to keep compilation manageable. Third and fourth cards repeat the verified milestones to reinforce practice: compiling small programs and inspecting VM output, and building simple OS interactions such as calling Output. printInt. Practice-driven verification helps connect theory to the compiled code and reveals how high-level structure maps to VM sequences.

screens.title: Jack language overview
screens.narratorSegment: Jack is a compact high-level language created for pedagogy. It borrows familiar Java-like syntax but intentionally keeps features small so you can implement a working compiler as part of the course. Define a class per file, use fields for instance storage, static for class storage, and write methods and constructors to operate on objects. A clear example is building a Main class with a function main that calls library routines such as Output. printInt. This design matters because it makes language, compiler, VM, and hardware responsibilities visible: the language expresses structure and intent, the compiler translates constructs into VM sequences, and the OS provides services like memory allocation and output. A common misconception is to think that Jack's small size limits the kinds of programs you can write; in practice you can implement complex algorithms and games because Jack remains Turing-complete. To practice, inspect a short Main. jack file and annotate declarations as either static, field, var, or parameter. That small exercise reveals how class structure maps to runtime storage and prepares you to read VM output later. How would you explain the purpose of a minimal language to a peer?

keyIdea.title: Jack overview
keyIdea.text: A deliberately small Java-like language designed so students can build a compiler and observe compilation results.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Jack language overview
Definition
Jack is a teaching language that is simple enough for a student-built compiler yet expressive enough to write games and utilities. It separates program structure into classes and methods and relies on a small OS for I/O and memory support.
Why this design
Simplifies compiler construction while preserving expressive power; you see how each construct compiles down to VM commands.
Common misconception
Small languages are not weak; Jack omits complexity to make compilation tractable for a course, yet it remains Turing-complete.
Analogy
Think of Jack as a blueprint language for programs: compact plans that a compiler translates into construction steps the VM executes.
Try this
Open a tiny .jack file and label each declaration as static, field, var, or parameter. Predict where each will live at runtime and check after compiling.

screens.title: Jack primitive and complex types
screens.narratorSegment: Jack's type system is intentionally small. The primitive types are int, boolean, and char. An int is a 16-bit signed integer and is used for arithmetic and counting. Boolean holds true or false values and controls branching. Char represents a single ASCII character. Beyond primitives, Jack supports arrays and object types. Arrays are created with Array. new and provide indexed storage for values; arrays are reference types so the variable holds an address. Objects are instances of classes; they are contiguous memory blocks whose base address serves as the object's identity. A concrete example: var int a; declares a local integer; Array a = Array. new(10); allocates a ten-element integer array and stores its reference. A common confusion is to treat arrays as primitive storage; in Jack they are objects with a base address and must be allocated via the OS. To practice, write a short snippet that creates an array of ten ints, stores values, and sums them. Observe how the compiler represents these operations in VM code: primitives map to simple push/pop operations while arrays and objects involve pointer manipulation and calls to OS routines. What does it change in your mental model to treat arrays as objects?

keyIdea.title: Types in Jack
keyIdea.text: Primitives are int, boolean, char. Arrays and objects are reference types that use base addresses and OS allocation.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Types
Primitive types
  • int: 16-bit signed integer used for arithmetic and indexing.
  • boolean: true or false, used for conditionals.
  • char: single ASCII character.
Complex types
Arrays and objects are reference types. Use Array.new to allocate arrays. Objects are instances of classes and are addressed by their base address.
Example
Array a = Array.new(10); // allocate an array of ten ints and store its reference in a
Practice
// create and sum an array
var Array arr;
let arr = Array.new(10);
let arr[0] = 1;
let arr[1] = 2;
// ... fill and sum
Remember: arrays require allocation via the OS; they are not raw contiguous stack storage like local variables. This affects how the compiler emits code for access and updates.

screens.title: Classes, files, and variable categories
screens.narratorSegment: Every Jack program is a collection of classes; each class resides in a separate. jack file. A class groups fields, static variables, and methods. Fields are per-instance storage; static variables belong to the class and are shared across all instances. Inside methods you declare local variables with var and accept parameters. Understanding these categories is essential because the compiler needs to assign each variable a memory segment at runtime. For example, a field maps to the this segment and lives in the object's memory block, while static variables are compiled to a static segment shared across instances. A concrete walkthrough: in a Point class you might declare field int x,y; a constructor allocates an object and initializes those fields; method getX returns x from the this segment. A common confusion is mixing field and local scopes: setting let x = ax inside the constructor assigns to the field when x is declared as a field, not to a new local variable. Practice by listing each variable in a sample class and labeling its storage segment: static, this, local, or argument. This mental mapping is the key step before reading VM code because the VM uses these segments directly.

keyIdea.title: Storage classes
keyIdea.text: Static, field, local, and parameter determine how variables are stored and accessed at runtime.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Classes & Variables
Class components
  • fields — object-level variables, accessed via this.
  • static — class-level shared variables.
  • methods/functions/constructors — behavior attached to the class or instances.
Variable kinds inside methods
local: var declarations; parameter: method arguments; both map to the stack frame and the VM local and argument segments.
Example: Point class storage
field int x,y; // stored in the object's memory block, accessed through this segment
Practice
Take a class with a constructor and list each declared variable with its runtime segment: static, this, local, or argument. Then match those to VM segments.

screens.title: Main.jack example walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a small, concrete Jack program and see how language constructs appear. The Main class defines a function main that declares local integers a, b, sum, assigns values, calls a function add, and prints the result. This example demonstrates variable declaration, call syntax, and a function return. The important lesson is how those high-level steps translate: local variables become VM local slots; a function call becomes push of arguments followed by a call command; return x+y becomes arithmetic and return from the VM viewpoint. For example, let a = 3 compiles to pushing the constant 3 then popping to the appropriate local variable. A common misconception is to expect fewer VM instructions for high-level statements; in fact the compiler expands statements into several VM commands to manage stack operations and call frames. Practice by compiling the add function in your head: returning x + y will push x and y, execute add, and return the result. After you write the Jack code, run the provided compiler and inspect the VM code to count the VM commands generated per Jack statement. That comparison reveals the mapping between language constructs and VM primitives.

keyIdea.title: From Jack to VM
keyIdea.text: A small Jack program quickly expands into VM operations; understanding the translation helps you inspect compiler output.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Main.jack Walkthrough
Example Jack code
// Main.jack
class Main {
    function void main() {
        var int a, b, sum;
        let a = 3;
        let b = 5;
        let sum = Main.add(a, b);
        do Output.printInt(sum);
        return;
    }
    function int add(int x, int y) {
        return x + y;
    }
}
Translate to VM (conceptual)
  • var declarations → allocate local slots in function frame.
  • let a = 3 → push constant 3; pop local a.
  • call Main.add → push arguments, call label, manage return address.
  • do Output.printInt(sum) → push argument, call OS routine, discard return value.
Check
Compile and count VM commands per Jack statement. Notice how one statement often expands to multiple VM operations.

screens.title: Methods, functions, and constructors
screens.narratorSegment: Jack distinguishes three kinds of routines: functions, methods, and constructors. A function is a class-level procedure that does not operate on an instance and therefore has no implicit this. A method is invoked on an object and receives the object reference as this, giving the method access to the object's fields via the this segment. A constructor builds a new object: it allocates memory, initializes fields, and then must return this. The requirement to end constructors with return this is important: the caller needs the object's base address to use the instance. Concretely, constructor Point new(int ax, int ay) calls Memory. alloc to reserve space for the fields, sets this to the new base address, initializes x and y, and returns this. A common misconception is to think constructors implicitly create a hidden object without explicit allocation; in Jack, allocation is explicit and visible in the compiled VM code. For practice, write a simple constructor and then inspect the VM sequence to find Memory. alloc, pointer setup, field initialization, and the return of this. Ask yourself: why must the constructor provide the object's address back to the caller?

keyIdea.title: Routine categories
keyIdea.text: Functions have no this, methods use this to access fields, constructors allocate and return a new object reference.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Routines & this
Kinds of routines
function: class-level, no implicit this.
method: operates on an instance; this points to the object's base.
constructor: allocates an object, initializes fields, and returns this.
Misconception
Constructors do not magically create objects; allocation and initialization appear in VM code and must return the object's address explicitly.
Concrete pattern
Constructor steps you will see in VM output: call Memory.alloc(n), set pointer to base, initialize fields by popping into this offsets, then push this and return.
Key Takeaway
Constructors must return this so the caller receives the object's base address and can use it for further calls and field access.

screens.title: Point.jack — object example
screens.narratorSegment: The Point class is a compact demonstration of object layout and methods. It declares field int x, y; then provides a constructor Point new(int ax, int ay) that assigns the fields from the parameters and returns this. Getter methods return field values and setters update them. This example makes two important points visible. First, fields live in the object memory block, so getX reads from this at the x offset and setX writes to that offset. Second, the constructor must allocate the object and return its base address so the caller can hold the reference. A common mistake is to expect getters and setters to use global storage; they use the this pointer and field offsets instead. Practically, inspect the compiled VM code for getX: you will see that it pushes the base address plus offset and then reads that memory location. For practice, create two Point objects, set their coordinates, and print them. When you compare VM output for two instances you will see identical method code but different this pointers used at call time. How does that observation help you reason about code reuse and memory layout?

keyIdea.title: Objects and fields
keyIdea.text: Fields are stored in an object's memory block; methods access them via the this pointer and offsets.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Point.jack Example
Point.jack source
// Point.jack
class Point {
    field int x, y;
    constructor Point new(int ax, int ay) {
        let x = ax;
        let y = ay;
        return this;
    }
    method int getX() { return x; }
    method int getY() { return y; }
    method void setX(int ax) { let x = ax; return; }
}
Memory model insight
Objects are contiguous memory blocks. The object's base address is passed as this; methods use this plus field offsets. The compiled code for methods is shared across instances; the only per-instance data is the this address and the object's fields.
Practice
Create two objects, call setX on each, and inspect VM output to see identical method code but different this pointers in calls.

screens.title: Control structures and statements
screens.narratorSegment: Jack includes the basic control and statement forms you need to write programs: let for assignment, do for calls that discard results, if-then-else for branching, while for loops, and return to exit routines. Each statement translates into a predictable VM pattern. For example, let a = expression compiles to evaluating the expression (pushing a result onto the stack) and then popping it to the target segment. The do statement pushes arguments, calls the routine, and then pops the return value into a temp to discard it. If statements compile to condition evaluation and conditional jumps to labels; while loops use label pairs for loop entry and exit. A frequent misconception is treating do and call as identical; do specifically discards any return value, so the compiler emits an extra pop. Practice by writing a small loop that sums numbers: the while condition checks an index variable, the body updates a sum using let, and the final result is returned or printed. Observing the VM output will show conditional jumps and label usage which are the primitive mechanisms by which high-level control flow is implemented. What distinction between do and let surprised you when inspecting VM output?

keyIdea.title: Control & statements
keyIdea.text: High-level statements map to VM primitives: pushes, pops, conditional jumps, and call/return sequences.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Control Structures
Statements
  • let: assignment — evaluate expression then pop into a target segment.
  • do: call a function and discard its return value.
  • if: evaluate condition, jump to then/else labels.
  • while: evaluate and jump back to loop label until false.
  • return: return a value or void from a routine.
Process example
To sum an array: initialize index and sum with let, loop with while, access elements by computing base+index, and use let to update sum. The compiler emits pushes and pops and labels for the loop control.
Common mistake
Expecting do to preserve a return value. do discards returns, so use let to capture a returned value if you need it.

screens.title: The Jack OS and standard libraries
screens.narratorSegment: Jack programs depend on a small operating system implemented in Jack itself. The OS provides a standard set of library functions: Memory for allocation, Array for array creation and access, Math for common numeric functions, String for manipulation, Output for printing, Screen for graphics, Keyboard for input, and Sys for system-level operations. Because the OS is written in Jack and compiled down the same way as user code, calling Output. printInt is implemented as a call to compiled routines and then VM-level commands that interact with the hardware abstraction layer. A practical consequence is that many language capabilities are built as library routines, not intrinsic language features — for example, array allocation is handled by the Array library rather than being built into the syntax. A common mistake is assuming OS routines are magic provided by the runtime; in this course you will implement parts of the OS to see exactly how those services are constructed. To practice, call Output. printInt from a small program and then inspect the compiled VM code for the call sequence and how the OS routine expects its arguments. What difference does it make to think of OS services as Jack code rather than built-in primitives?

screens.title: What Jack omits and why
screens.narratorSegment: Jack deliberately omits many features common in industrial languages. Missing features include floating-point types, for and switch control constructs, break/continue, class inheritance and polymorphism, generics, pointer arithmetic, exceptions, and automatic garbage collection. The reason is not ignorance but pedagogy: each omitted feature greatly increases the complexity of parsing, type checking, code generation, and runtime management. For example, adding inheritance would require implementing method dispatch tables and complex layout rules; adding floating point would require hardware or software support and new runtime routines. A frequent student question is whether these omissions make Jack unrealistic; the answer is that the omissions make Jack implementable by hand in a single course while still allowing you to explore core concepts. A practical assessment: list three features you think would be the hardest to add to Jack and explain why. That thought exercise sharpens your sense of compiler complexity and helps you appreciate design trade-offs when language designers choose which features to include. What Jack omits and why means jack omits complex language features so the compiler and runtime remain implementable by students while preserving expressive power.. In practical terms, a concise comparison with larger languages and the pedagogical rationale. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
Jack is the small, Java-like language used throughout this course to teach compilation and object-oriented design. It gives you familiar ideas — classes, methods, constructors, arrays — but keeps the syntax and feature set deliberately minimal so you can build a compiler for it by hand. In practical terms, Jack programs are split into. jack files, each defining a class with fields and methods. That simplicity makes Jack an ideal learning target: you can write a game such as Pong using Jack, compile it to VM code, then to machine code, and see how high-level ideas become concrete instructions. A concrete example is the Main class that calls Output. printInt to display values. A common misconception is that a small language cannot express complex algorithms — in fact Jack is Turing-complete, so brevity does not mean weakness; Jack just limits surface complexity so implementation stays feasible. As you move through these screens you will learn Jack's types, variable kinds, method categories, object construction, and how the Jack OS supplies basic services. Think about this question as we start: what is the smallest set of language features you need to express a complete program?

These objectives describe the core knowledge you will build. First, you will be able to describe Jack's syntax and semantics: that means naming its primitive types, the role of classes and methods, and how source files map to classes. As an example, you should be able to read a simple class file and identify fields, methods, and constructors. Second, you will understand Jack's type system: int, boolean, char, arrays, and objects, and why Jack restricts itself to a small set. Being able to explain the type choices helps you see how compilers perform type checking and memory layout. A common misconception is to assume small type systems are too weak; instead, they simplify compilation while remaining expressive. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify your understanding by reading a short Jack file and tracing variable storage. Practice by opening a Main. jack file, locating each declaration, and describing the storage class. That active check helps cement the objective before you move to applying Jack in programs.

These objectives focus on what you will be able to do. First, you will write simple Jack programs using variables, expressions, and control structures and compile them to VM code. A practical check is to write a calculator program and compare the generated VM commands for each Jack statement. Second, you will explain and use Jack's object features: write classes with fields and constructors, create objects, and call methods that use this. The constructor pattern—allocating memory and returning this—is important, and you will see how it appears in the VM code. A typical misconception is to equate Jack classes with full Java classes including inheritance; Jack deliberately omits inheritance and polymorphism to keep compilation manageable. Third and fourth cards repeat the verified milestones to reinforce practice: compiling small programs and inspecting VM output, and building simple OS interactions such as calling Output. printInt. Practice-driven verification helps connect theory to the compiled code and reveals how high-level structure maps to VM sequences.

Jack is a compact high-level language created for pedagogy. It borrows familiar Java-like syntax but intentionally keeps features small so you can implement a working compiler as part of the course. Define a class per file, use fields for instance storage, static for class storage, and write methods and constructors to operate on objects. A clear example is building a Main class with a function main that calls library routines such as Output. printInt. This design matters because it makes language, compiler, VM, and hardware responsibilities visible: the language expresses structure and intent, the compiler translates constructs into VM sequences, and the OS provides services like memory allocation and output. A common misconception is to think that Jack's small size limits the kinds of programs you can write; in practice you can implement complex algorithms and games because Jack remains Turing-complete. To practice, inspect a short Main. jack file and annotate declarations as either static, field, var, or parameter. That small exercise reveals how class structure maps to runtime storage and prepares you to read VM output later. How would you explain the purpose of a minimal language to a peer?

Jack's type system is intentionally small. The primitive types are int, boolean, and char. An int is a 16-bit signed integer and is used for arithmetic and counting. Boolean holds true or false values and controls branching. Char represents a single ASCII character. Beyond primitives, Jack supports arrays and object types. Arrays are created with Array. new and provide indexed storage for values; arrays are reference types so the variable holds an address. Objects are instances of classes; they are contiguous memory blocks whose base address serves as the object's identity. A concrete example: var int a; declares a local integer; Array a = Array. new(10); allocates a ten-element integer array and stores its reference. A common confusion is to treat arrays as primitive storage; in Jack they are objects with a base address and must be allocated via the OS. To practice, write a short snippet that creates an array of ten ints, stores values, and sums them. Observe how the compiler represents these operations in VM code: primitives map to simple push/pop operations while arrays and objects involve pointer manipulation and calls to OS routines. What does it change in your mental model to treat arrays as objects?

Every Jack program is a collection of classes; each class resides in a separate. jack file. A class groups fields, static variables, and methods. Fields are per-instance storage; static variables belong to the class and are shared across all instances. Inside methods you declare local variables with var and accept parameters. Understanding these categories is essential because the compiler needs to assign each variable a memory segment at runtime. For example, a field maps to the this segment and lives in the object's memory block, while static variables are compiled to a static segment shared across instances. A concrete walkthrough: in a Point class you might declare field int x,y; a constructor allocates an object and initializes those fields; method getX returns x from the this segment. A common confusion is mixing field and local scopes: setting let x = ax inside the constructor assigns to the field when x is declared as a field, not to a new local variable. Practice by listing each variable in a sample class and labeling its storage segment: static, this, local, or argument. This mental mapping is the key step before reading VM code because the VM uses these segments directly.

Let's walk through a small, concrete Jack program and see how language constructs appear. The Main class defines a function main that declares local integers a, b, sum, assigns values, calls a function add, and prints the result. This example demonstrates variable declaration, call syntax, and a function return. The important lesson is how those high-level steps translate: local variables become VM local slots; a function call becomes push of arguments followed by a call command; return x+y becomes arithmetic and return from the VM viewpoint. For example, let a = 3 compiles to pushing the constant 3 then popping to the appropriate local variable. A common misconception is to expect fewer VM instructions for high-level statements; in fact the compiler expands statements into several VM commands to manage stack operations and call frames. Practice by compiling the add function in your head: returning x + y will push x and y, execute add, and return the result. After you write the Jack code, run the provided compiler and inspect the VM code to count the VM commands generated per Jack statement. That comparison reveals the mapping between language constructs and VM primitives.

Jack distinguishes three kinds of routines: functions, methods, and constructors. A function is a class-level procedure that does not operate on an instance and therefore has no implicit this. A method is invoked on an object and receives the object reference as this, giving the method access to the object's fields via the this segment. A constructor builds a new object: it allocates memory, initializes fields, and then must return this. The requirement to end constructors with return this is important: the caller needs the object's base address to use the instance. Concretely, constructor Point new(int ax, int ay) calls Memory. alloc to reserve space for the fields, sets this to the new base address, initializes x and y, and returns this. A common misconception is to think constructors implicitly create a hidden object without explicit allocation; in Jack, allocation is explicit and visible in the compiled VM code. For practice, write a simple constructor and then inspect the VM sequence to find Memory. alloc, pointer setup, field initialization, and the return of this. Ask yourself: why must the constructor provide the object's address back to the caller?

The Point class is a compact demonstration of object layout and methods. It declares field int x, y; then provides a constructor Point new(int ax, int ay) that assigns the fields from the parameters and returns this. Getter methods return field values and setters update them. This example makes two important points visible. First, fields live in the object memory block, so getX reads from this at the x offset and setX writes to that offset. Second, the constructor must allocate the object and return its base address so the caller can hold the reference. A common mistake is to expect getters and setters to use global storage; they use the this pointer and field offsets instead. Practically, inspect the compiled VM code for getX: you will see that it pushes the base address plus offset and then reads that memory location. For practice, create two Point objects, set their coordinates, and print them. When you compare VM output for two instances you will see identical method code but different this pointers used at call time. How does that observation help you reason about code reuse and memory layout?

Jack includes the basic control and statement forms you need to write programs: let for assignment, do for calls that discard results, if-then-else for branching, while for loops, and return to exit routines. Each statement translates into a predictable VM pattern. For example, let a = expression compiles to evaluating the expression (pushing a result onto the stack) and then popping it to the target segment. The do statement pushes arguments, calls the routine, and then pops the return value into a temp to discard it. If statements compile to condition evaluation and conditional jumps to labels; while loops use label pairs for loop entry and exit. A frequent misconception is treating do and call as identical; do specifically discards any return value, so the compiler emits an extra pop. Practice by writing a small loop that sums numbers: the while condition checks an index variable, the body updates a sum using let, and the final result is returned or printed. Observing the VM output will show conditional jumps and label usage which are the primitive mechanisms by which high-level control flow is implemented. What distinction between do and let surprised you when inspecting VM output?

Jack programs depend on a small operating system implemented in Jack itself. The OS provides a standard set of library functions: Memory for allocation, Array for array creation and access, Math for common numeric functions, String for manipulation, Output for printing, Screen for graphics, Keyboard for input, and Sys for system-level operations. Because the OS is written in Jack and compiled down the same way as user code, calling Output. printInt is implemented as a call to compiled routines and then VM-level commands that interact with the hardware abstraction layer. A practical consequence is that many language capabilities are built as library routines, not intrinsic language features — for example, array allocation is handled by the Array library rather than being built into the syntax. A common mistake is assuming OS routines are magic provided by the runtime; in this course you will implement parts of the OS to see exactly how those services are constructed. To practice, call Output. printInt from a small program and then inspect the compiled VM code for the call sequence and how the OS routine expects its arguments. What difference does it make to think of OS services as Jack code rather than built-in primitives?

Jack deliberately omits many features common in industrial languages. Missing features include floating-point types, for and switch control constructs, break/continue, class inheritance and polymorphism, generics, pointer arithmetic, exceptions, and automatic garbage collection. The reason is not ignorance but pedagogy: each omitted feature greatly increases the complexity of parsing, type checking, code generation, and runtime management. For example, adding inheritance would require implementing method dispatch tables and complex layout rules; adding floating point would require hardware or software support and new runtime routines. A frequent student question is whether these omissions make Jack unrealistic; the answer is that the omissions make Jack implementable by hand in a single course while still allowing you to explore core concepts. A practical assessment: list three features you think would be the hardest to add to Jack and explain why. That thought exercise sharpens your sense of compiler complexity and helps you appreciate design trade-offs when language designers choose which features to include. What Jack omits and why means jack omits complex language features so the compiler and runtime remain implementable by students while preserving expressive power.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

First, Hello World exercises string and output routines in the OS; it tests calling Output. printString or equivalent. Second, Calculator reads two numbers from the keyboard, computes their sum, and prints the result; it exercises input, local variables, arithmetic, and Output. printInt. Third, Array sum creates an array of ten integers, fills it, and sums them; this checks array creation via Array. new, indexed access, loops, and accumulation.
